segments.text: In March this year, many ClaudeCode users began to complain that their agent felt dumber than before.
Now, this has been a common, timeless, and unprovable complaint, the they don't make things like they used to of the AI world, if you will.
But in early April, a 4.5,000 word GitHub post, changed all of that.
Stella Lorenzo, a senior director of AI at AMD, came with receipts.
She used data from almost 7,000 ClaudeCode sessions to comprehensively demonstrate,
the agent's regression. In fact, her work was so compelling that it led to an anthropic
investigation and a public report detailing their findings and fixes. This story is really
instructive, so let's follow the data, her conclusions, and then how to build a similar early
warning system for your own agents, so that the next time something like this happens, you're not
flying blind. We all love a good detective story, whether it's Sherlock Holmes, Nancy Drew,
or Detective Pikachu. My favorite part of Lorenzo's analysis,
was that she figured all of this stuff out from the analysis of local session logs produced
by Claude Code. Across three months, the AMD team had logged 6,800 sessions, 17,000 thinking
blocks and over 230,000 tool calls. She broke the starter down into periods that she called
the good, transitional, and degraded. For simplicity, let's talk about the stats across two of those
periods, the good and the degraded. Between those two, the agents read activity to edit
activity ratio collapsed from 6.6 reads per edit during the good period to just two during
the degraded period, meaning that on average, the agent was fact-gathering 70% less often before making
changes. And shared plenty of other stats too. The post also demonstrates that edits without
any reading, circular loops, and premature stopping all occurred significantly more often than
before. And it wasn't just quantitative stats either. Qualitative metrics like manual user interrupts,
rose sharply, and Claude began describing its own in-chat work as lazy, rushed or sloppy.
And to top all of that, as the output quality went down, their token usage went up, way up,
in fact. Between February and March, she estimates that the daily usage in tokens increased by a factor
of over 100 for a similar number of prompts. Now, to be fair, there are mitigating circumstances.
It wasn't just the agent using more tokens by itself. She explains that some of the token increase
was due to very excited engineers spinning up further subagents. But the result was still pretty
bad since they were now trying to do more with degraded agents. She sums up the change from an
engineer's perspective going from, I can run 50 agents and they all produce excellent work, to every
single one of these agents is now an idiot. In fact, she found that thinking blocks were about 70% shorter
in the degraded period than the good period. This is really important because as she points out, the model
being able to spend tokens to think deeply is key to solving these complex problems.
Although they had no way of knowing why, this was amazing detective work to prove degradation
of Claude Code during this period. Reading her post made me very curious about my own agents. Would I even
know if their behavior ever changed? How will I achieve my dream of delegating my work to agents
and spending more time gaming if I can't even do that? So I decided to take a look.
One experiment I ran was to build a reverse proxy that sits between
my coding agents and the model so it can pause the traffic and ship everything to Elastic
search. I pointed it at a few different harnesses doing the same task and started poking
around. Within one day, the data turned up something really surprising. Two harnesses with
similar token usage on the same task had vastly different bills. One was costing
almost three times as much as the other. That seemed so odd that my first thought was that I
had met something up. But an online search led me to this GitHub pull request, flagging a prompt
caching bug in open code. And the behavior matched. Under certain conditions, open code could
miss the cache, which means slower inference and dramatically higher cost, exactly what I was seeing
in the data. Look, you're not always going to find little gems like this, and I was probably quite
lucky here to come across the bug in my tiny demo for a video. It's like buying a Lego dinosaur
and finding a real fossil inside. It shouldn't really happen, but I'll take it.
Now the point here isn't the bug. Bugs are a fact of life, and I still think open code's amazing.
But it does make me wonder, what else might you find if you looked?
Now, a bespoke proxy isn't great for production. You're running a separate process,
adding a network hop, managing certs and auth. And the proxy itself needs to be maintained,
which isn't trivial even when vibe coding. In some ways, especially vibe coding, but I digress.
The deeper problem is conceptual. A proxy sits between the harness and the model. It can see the traffic,
but it has zero visibility into the harness. Internal state, tool, tool execution detail,
errors handling, all of these things are invisible. You're still treating the harness as
a black box. What you actually want is instrumentation inside the harness, and that's where
open telemetry comes in. Open telemetry or OTEL is a standardized observability framework
for emitting traces, metrics and logs. The major coding agents like ClaudeCode, OpenAI Codex,
and Gemini CLI have first-party OTEL output built in. And others like OpenCode and Pi have plugins
or extensions for the same thing.
news is you don't have to be an expert to set this up. I was able to wire my coding agent's
hotel extension using the docs and elastic agent skills in less than an hour so that all usage
data is sent to this in the elastic instance. And this is my resulting dashboard. Let's view it through
the lens of which parts of this dashboard might have caught the degradations seen by Lorenzo.
At the top, I've got the global usage stats, sessions, turns, tool calls and failures. Useful
as a baseline, but I think the next parts are even more meaningful.
This panel shows stop reasons over time. So did the turn end on a tool call? Did the model
finished naturally or did I manually stop it? A spike in this last category of manual
stoppage is exactly what AMD would have seen as engineers saw the model doing the wrong
thing and yank the chain. Now the read to edit ratio reduction was a key stat as you remember,
and this chart shows exactly that. We also have a chart that breaks down tool calls by type
alongside the read to edit ratio over time. So if something changes, whether it's the model, the harness, the service
site update or so on, I'd expect this ratio to move. And here, I've got tool outcomes over
time. So if something starts breaking tool calls, a model regression, a flaky plug-in, new
permission setup, what have you, the failure rate should climb here. And I also track the tool
call patterns so that if a tool isn't being called when it should, or if it's data usage patterns change,
I'll see those here. And the nice thing is, the dashboard doesn't need to be perfect straight
away, that's the beauty of having the underlying logs and metrics inelastic. I can build whatever
dashboard I need later and run any in-depth analysis on the raw data when I notice something
is off. The point is that this gives you a real-time display. Look, streaming a dashboard isn't going
to win a lot of viewers on Twitch, but it's probably more useful than yet another gaming channel.
If a model update shifts behavior, if a server site cache bug degrades context, or if a harness update
changes defaults, I should see it in these trend lines. Before we move on, I'd love to know what you
thought about these dashboards, what's good, what's bad, or what's missing. I'm also considering
videos on setting up telemetry for major harnesses like Codex or Claude Code, so I'd love to hear from
you, which will help us plan these. And on the way to the comments, give us a like, it'll help to keep
me employed and help others to find these videos. But let's come back to where we started and close
the loop on Roezo's story. Just turned her month after her post, Anthropic published their report.
It turned out that multiple things had changed simultaneously.
One, the harness had changed.
The default reasoning effort parameter went from high to medium, which affected a lot of people.
Two, the new Opus model introduced something called adaptive thinking, which lets the model decide
its own thinking budget.
This is a great idea for efficiency, but it had a side effect of sometimes deciding not to think
at all.
Three, and probably the most significant, was a server-side bug.
Anthropic had introduced a calculation.
caching efficiency feature that would discard all thinking blocks on resumption after a month.
But this bug meant that once this feature was triggered, it silently dropped all thinking blocks
from subsequent message histories.
And without the thinking blocks, the model just didn't have enough context while missing the
cache, which both degraded performance and increased cost.
From the user perspective, these all happened at similar times with little visibility.
I can imagine it being a frustrating experience for everyone with little proof that something was even
wrong. Except, of course, for Stella Lorenzo. The difference between her and everybody
else was that she looked into logs, performed rigorous analysis and identified what was going on.
Now, up until this point, I've been telling you how wonderful logs are, but of course there are some
trade-offs, so let's talk about that. One, session logs generate real data and retention costs money.
As always, with observability, you should keep an eye on the volume your team is generating
and decide what to log and how long to keep it for.
If Timmy over there in your team is constantly spawning 50 sub-agents for a random side project
that runs all week or using open call to troll reditors, maybe that doesn't need as much retention
as the data from agents working on your company's main product.
Two, real risk of leakage. These logs can capture confidential information and credentials
and become on yet another potential tax surface and liability. So make sure that you don't create
any more risks than you have to. You could exclude message bodies, log metadata or mechral
tricks only, or have custom sanitization logic. None of these are perfect, but you should see
what makes sense for you. When building these demos, I saw my agent execute shell commands with
credentials right in them, which would not get redacted and end up in the logs. I should shamelessly plug, though,
that that's another reason for going with a proven product like Lastic with great granular security
and access control. Three, this gets set up, but never looked at again. Build a habit of looking at it
and set up alerts on the signals that matter to you, so you don't have to manually
look at them all the time. The lesson for me from all of this is that every session generates
signal. Right now, your agent is making decisions you can't see, using a harness that grows
more complex all the time, shaped by service-side parameters, thousands of kilometers away from
you. And unless you're capturing that signal, you're really flying blind. Oytel support is built
into major harnesses, or just one plug-in away. An elastic gives you somewhere secure and easy to use
to send it, monitor it, and investigate it. Your coding agent is a black box, but it doesn't
have to stay that way. Thanks for watching. I read every comment, so please let me know if you have
any questions. Like I said, give us a like if you can. It helps others to find our video. And if you didn't
like it, that's fine too. If you let us know why, that'll help us improve. Thanks for watching.
See you next time.
